title: Entered password on a phishing page
symptom: User typed their work password into a fake sign-in page from an email link
user_description: I clicked a link in an email about a shared invoice and it asked me to sign in, so I did. Then the page just went blank. My colleague says it was probably fake. What do I do?

options.text: Tell him to delete the email and carry on, since nothing seems to have happened
options.why: The attacker may already have the password. Deleting the email does nothing to stop them signing in.

options.text: Just run an antivirus scan on his PC
options.why: A fake sign-in page steals the password itself. A scan of the PC does not stop someone using that password from anywhere.

options.text: Reset his password now, sign him out of all sessions, check his MFA methods and mailbox rules for anything new, then escalate to the security team
options.why: Acting fast locks the attacker out. Attackers often add their own MFA method or a forwarding rule, so checking those matters, and the security team needs to know in case others got the same email.

options.text: Wait and see if anything unusual happens on his account
options.why: By the time something unusual shows, the attacker may have read mail, sent more phishing or stolen data.

hints: Does the attacker already have something they can use?
Can an attacker stay signed in even after one change?
Who else needs to know about this email?
real_world_tip: Ask the user when they clicked and keep the original email (as an attachment, not forwarded as a link) for the security team. Never ask for or write down the password they typed.

escalation.team_why: A stolen password is a security incident. The security team can check the sign-in logs, find anyone else who got the same email and block the sender.

details.text: When he clicked the link and signed in
details.why: The team checks the sign-in logs from that moment onwards.

details.text: The sender's address, with the email attached as a file (not forwarded as a link)
details.why: Lets them block the sender and find everyone else who received it.

details.text: What he typed into the page (his work email and password)
details.why: Tells them what the attacker may now have, without writing the password itself down.

details.text: What you have already done (password reset, sessions signed out)
details.why: Saves time and stops them repeating steps or missing one.

details.text: The password he typed, so they can check it
details.why: Never write a password in a ticket or email. They only need to know it was entered, and you have already reset it.
Has nothing to do with the incident. Only share personal details when they are needed.
